title: Bhai Randhir Singh
hook: a revolutionary and devotee whose followers founded the Akhand Kirtani Jatha

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing the Rehat Maryada, and your line was a code, agreed. Did you write your three lines? Today, a man who kept his own code inside a prison. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

A guard's footsteps go down a stone corridor at night, past an iron door, and fade. From behind the door comes a voice singing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib, steady and unhurried, as if the room were a gurdwara. The guards have heard it before. They will hear it again tomorrow. The man singing has been sentenced for plotting against the British government, and he has many years still to serve. The singing does not stop. Today: Bhai Randhir Singh.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS IN A STONE CORRIDOR.` → `A VOICE SINGING SHABADS.` → `THE SINGING DOES NOT STOP.`

segments.voice: First, the two sides of him. Bhai Randhir Singh came from the village of Narangwal in Punjab. He was drawn into the Ghadar plans against British rule that we met earlier in this block, and he was arrested and given a long prison sentence. He was a revolutionary. He was also, before and after, a man of deep devotion. Second, the rehat in jail. In jail he was expected to eat what he was given and live as the jail decided. He held to his own strict discipline as a Khalsa Sikh, including about the food he would accept, and when it was refused he went without, for long stretches. His own account of these years, his Jail Letters, describes the hunger, the punishments and the stubbornness in plain terms. Third, the singing. Through all of it he kept up kirtan, singing the Gurus' hymns, alone or with any Sikh prisoner who would join him. That's today's line: kirtan in prison. Fourth, the root and the fruit. At Ang 1075 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that in this dark age, kirtan, singing the Lord's praise, is supreme. After his release, those who gathered around Bhai Randhir Singh formed the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, known for kirtan that can go on through the whole night, and for a strict rehat of their own. Some Sikhs follow that path closely; others admire it from a distance. Either way, it began in a cell, with one voice that wouldn't stop singing.
screen: `REVOLUTIONARY AND DEVOTEE.` · `HE KEPT HIS REHAT IN JAIL.` · `HE KEPT SINGING.` · `KIRTAN THROUGH THE NIGHT.` · then, large: `KIRTAN IN PRISON.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a song. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind something hard you're carrying right now: a worry, a loss, a situation you can't leave. Then let a song come to mind, one that steadies you. A shabad, a hymn, a lullaby, anything. You don't have to sing aloud. Hum it quietly, or hear it inside, line by line, while the hard thing sits beside you. Let the song keep its own pace. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the song, on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Randhir Singh. A revolutionary and devotee who kept his rehat and his kirtan through long years in prison, and whose followers founded the Akhand Kirtani Jatha. Today's word.
Your line: kirtan in prison. Today, sing through a hardship: when something heavy comes, hum one steady song, even under your breath. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: The Akhand Kirtani Jatha holds kirtan programs, including all-night kirtan, and its members keep a strict rehat; Bhai Randhir Singh's writings, including his prison letters, are read among his followers and others.

notes: Editor: cut the superlative 'the hardest place there is' from the review; varied the hook's opening (too many hooks in this stretch open on a bare noun phrase) and replaced 'not singing to pass the time', which claimed his motive, with 'the singing does not stop'; fixed the garbled 'Prison tried to make him eat'.
